extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and foundations of geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of the epistemic status of geometric first principles and axioms, and of whether they are hypotheses derived from experience or a priori necessary truths. The text examines how to treat definitions, axioms, hypotheses, mental imagery, and the psychological sources of our conviction in such principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation for scientific convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific convenience, confine attention to those properties of an object that are material to the investigation (e.g., geometrical properties), and formally treat the object as if divested of other properties when those properties have no practical necessity for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological expedient: we are still thinking of real objects with all their properties, but 'feign' them divested of irrelevant properties. Warning: it is an error to suppose we actually conceive the object devoid of its other properties; suppressed properties must be restored when and insofar as their presence or absence would materially affect conclusions (examples: thermal expansion affecting figure and magnitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat first principles of geometry as hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called first principles (as involved in definitions) of geometry are to be regarded as hypotheses: statements assumed for the sake of tracing consequences rather than exact correspondences with fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their apparent certainty is derived from the role they play in deductive reasoning, not from their being literally true of nature. This is the position attributed to Dugald Stewart and defended against Whewell's objections in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity in deductive sciences = derivability from suppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'necessity' of conclusions in deductive sciences consists in their correctly following from the suppositions from which they are deduced, not necessarily in their absolute truth about the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, deductive conclusions are 'necessary' only conditional on the initial assumptions; similar 'necessity' could be obtained in any field by reasoning from chosen hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must relate to real existents and avoid distinct falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses used for scientific inquiry must relate to something that has real existence and must not ascribe distinctly false properties to the thing under study; permitted liberties are slight exaggeration of actual properties and suppression of irrelevant ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The liberty extends only to assuming objects to be completely what they are 'very nearly' and suppressing other properties, but always under the obligation to restore them where they matter. Arbitrary hypotheses about nonexisting entities may be useful intellectually but do not add to knowledge of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include axioms among first principles; some axioms are indemonstrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Among first principles we must admit axioms as well as definitions; some axioms are fundamental and not capable of demonstration (e.g., 'Two straight lines which coincide in two points coincide altogether' or Playfair's parallel property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some axioms can be recast or proved from others by constructions (imaginary superposition), there remain a few fundamental indemonstrable truths that must be admitted in any geometrical system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish axioms that are true without hypothesis from definitional premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms differ from principles involved in definitions in that axioms may be true without any mixture of hypothesis, whereas definitional premises are hypothetical simplifications or conveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geometric axioms can be as true of real lines and figures as of imagined ones; other sciences similarly have some exact general propositions (e.g., Newton's first law) alongside approximations that require feigning exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are experimental generalizations (empirical origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground of our belief in axioms is experimental: axioms are generalizations from observation (induction) rather than pure a priori truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that propositions like 'two straight lines cannot inclose a space' are inductions from sensory evidence and receive continual confirmation from observation; thus experience can account for the strong conviction we have in some axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental imagery can function as experimental evidence when faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact mental pictures (imaginary diagrams) may serve as legitimate subjects of geometrical experimentation, because our ideas of form can resemble sensations so closely that reasoning about mental images parallels reasoning about physical diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows us to 'see' geometric truths by thinking of lines and figures, provided long experience has shown that such images faithfully represent real objects (analogy: a daguerreotype picture representing the original). This also addresses the issue of 'infinite' extension by imagining the prolongation and inspecting the mental image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability does not prove metaphysical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the negation of a proposition is inconceivable to us does not establish that the proposition is metaphysically necessary, because our capacity to conceive is heavily shaped by past experience and associative habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (antipodes, Newtonian gravity, etc.) show that what once seemed inconceivable can later be readily conceived and accepted; thus inconceivableness is an unreliable marker of necessary truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological proof needed to establish a priori origin of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that axioms are a priori (i.e., known independently of experience), one would have to show chronologically that conviction in them preceded relevant sensory impressions; this is generally impossible to demonstrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such chronological proof is out of reach (origin too far back for memory/observation), the burden of proof lies on advocates of a priori accounts, and the default explanation favors experiential origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association and habit can make empirical truths seem necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated experience and the laws of association can cause propositions learned by observation to take on the appearance of necessary and inconceivable truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses psychological explanation: when two facts are habitually observed together, later generations may find it 'inconceivable' to separate them. Whewell's own historical examples illustrate how previously non-intuitive scientific truths come to be viewed as self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish necessity from contingency by conceivability, but with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary truth is commonly defined as one whose negation is inconceivable; however, because conceivability is influenced by mental habits and experience, this test must be applied cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical relations (e.g., 3 + 2 = 5) are cited as instances where negation is inconceivable; yet the text warns that this criterion can mislead when applied to first principles that are rooted in habitual observation rather than pure a priori insight.
